name: Digital Fairness Act (proposed)
impact_assessment: full: SWD(2026) 1101 (Regulatory Scrutiny Board: positive with reservations, 3 July 2026)

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Impact assessment report accompanying the Digital Fairness Act and the simplification of consumer protection rules, SWD(2026) 1101
literature.title: Impact assessment report: Digital Fairness Act and simplification of consumer protection rules
literature.headline: The Commission's impact assessment for the Digital Fairness Act and the Consumer Rights Directive simplification; the Commission expects the consumer package to save EU consumers up to EUR 13.7 billion a year. The Regulatory Scrutiny Board gave a positive opinion with reservations on 3 July 2026.
literature.verified: proposal explanatory memorandum and press release read; report itself not yet read

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Fitness check of EU consumer law on digital fairness, SWD(2024) 230
literature.title: Fitness check of EU consumer law on digital fairness
literature.headline: Existing EU consumer law does not adequately address dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation and subscription traps; the basis for the Digital Fairness Act.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Public consultation on the Digital Fairness Act: Factual summary report, Ares(2025)11521347, 22 December 2025
literature.title: Public consultation on the Digital Fairness Act: Factual summary report
literature.outcomes: stakeholder views on new EU action
literature.headline: 3,341 responses (1,733 outside one consumer campaign of 1,594; 74% of them consumers): 72% back new binding rules on dark patterns and 70% on addictive design; large companies show little support for new action on specific dark patterns (14-22%), SMEs more (32-73%). A separate call for evidence drew 4,325 responses.
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's summary of who answered its Digital Fairness Act consultation and what they said: most respondents, mainly consumers, want new binding rules, while large companies largely see no need for new action.

literature.citation: BEUC (2025), Towards the Digital Fairness Act, BEUC-X-2025-110
literature.title: Towards the Digital Fairness Act
literature.headline: Calls for a general ban on dark patterns and blacklisting common ones, an 'average consumer' concept that reflects vulnerability online, and a shift of the burden of proof to businesses.

literature.citation: NERA (2025), European Commission Digital Fairness Act, NERA insight
literature.title: European Commission Digital Fairness Act
literature.headline: Design choices involve trade-offs between consumers and businesses, so the impact assessment should weigh net consumer welfare; worked examples on junk fees and subscription cancellation.

literature.citation: Bitkom (2025), Position paper: A Digital Fairness Act, Bitkom
literature.title: Position paper: A Digital Fairness Act
literature.headline: Calls for an economic impact assessment and questions the need for new rules given the DSA, GDPR, Data Act and AI Act; argues 'dark patterns' is not clearly defined.
literature.interested_party: Bitkom, the German digital industry association

literature.citation: Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (Ireland) (2025), Submission to the European Commission's Digital Fairness Act consultation, CCPC
literature.title: Submission to the European Commission's Digital Fairness Act consultation
literature.headline: Supports the aims; asks for a defined list of dark patterns and opt-in for addictive features.

literature.citation: European Parliamentary Research Service (2026), Towards a digital fairness act, EPRS briefing
literature.title: Towards a digital fairness act
literature.headline: Parliament's research service briefing on the planned Digital Fairness Act.
